result.topic_en: Entries from Gauss's mathematical diary (March 1797) comparing the integrals of $e^{-t^a}$ and $1/\sqrt[b]{1+u^c}$, and recording several results about dividing the lemniscate and about the lemniscatic sine, including the constant $e^{\pi/2}$.
result.transcription:
Formularum integralium formae
$\int e^{-t^a}dt$ et $\int\frac{du}{\sqrt[b]{(1+u^c)}}$
inter se comparationem institui. Mrz 2.
Cur [-...-] ad aequationem perveniatur
gradus $nn$ ti dividendo curvam lemni-
scatam in $n$ partes ... Mrt. 19
A potestatibus integr. $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(1-x^4)}}^{(0-1)}$ pendet
$\Sigma\left(\frac{mm+6mn+nn}{(mm+nn)^4}\right)^k$
Lemniscata geometrice in quinque
partes dividitur Mrt. 21.
Inter multa alia Curvam lemniscatam
spectantia observavi Numeratorem sinus
decompositi, arcus duplicis esse =
2 Num. Denom. sinus $\times$ Num. Den. Cos. arcus simpl.
Denominatorem vero =
Num. sin.$^4$ + Denom. sin.$^4$. Iam si {+hic+} Deno-
minator pro arcu $\pi'$ ponatur $\theta$ erit Denom.
sin arcus $k\pi'$, $=\theta^{kk}$. Iam $\theta = 4,810480$
cuius numeri logarithmus hyperbolicus est =
1,570796 i.e. $=\frac12\pi$ quod maxime est memorabile
cuiusque proprietatis demonstratio gravissima
analyseos incrementa [-...-] pollicetur. Mrt. 29.

items.english: Why does one arrive at an equation of degree n² when dividing the lemniscate curve into n parts?
The sum Σ((mm+6mn+nn)/(mm+nn)^4)^k depends on powers of the integral ∫dx/√(1−x⁴) (from 0 to 1).

items.quote:
Lemniscata geometrice in quinque
partes dividitur
items.english: The lemniscate is divided geometrically into five parts.

items.english: Now if here the denominator for the arc π' is set equal to θ, the denominator of the sine of the arc kπ' will be θ^{kk}. Now θ = 4.810480, whose natural logarithm is 1.570796, i.e. ½π.
